lead: A Maxwell relation turns an entropy derivative you cannot measure into a pressure–volume–temperature slope you can. It exists because every thermodynamic potential — internal energy, enthalpy, Helmholtz function, Gibbs function — has an exact differential, and exactness forces the two mixed second derivatives to be equal. That single fact yields four equations. Engineers use them to compute entropy changes from p-v-T data, to build the enthalpy departure term in real-gas charts, and to predict whether a gas cools or warms when it is throttled through a valve.
prereq: You need: 4.3 for the exact differentials of A and G, and Unit 3 for entropy as a state property.

sections.h3: Exact differentials make mixed derivatives equal

blocks.text: Internal energy U is a state property: the change between two states is the same whatever path the gas took. Its differential is therefore exact. For a simple compressible system, with two independent properties:

blocks.where: U is internal energy in kJ, T is absolute temperature in K, S is entropy in kJ/K, p is pressure in kPa and V is volume in m³.

blocks.text: Euler's criterion says: if dz = M dx + N dy is exact, then (∂M/∂y)<sub>x</sub> = (∂N/∂x)<sub>y</sub>. The subscript names the variable held constant. The criterion is only the statement that the two mixed second derivatives of z are equal, since both are ∂²z/∂x∂y.
Match terms. The coefficient of dS is T, so M = T and x = S. The coefficient of dV is −p, so N = −p and y = V. Applying the criterion:

blocks.where: the left side is the rate of change of temperature with volume at constant entropy; the right side is minus the rate of change of pressure with entropy at constant volume.

blocks.text: That is the first Maxwell relation. It is not a new law, only the exactness of dU written out. Its value is that it swaps one partial derivative for another, so a quantity you cannot measure is replaced by one you can.

items: Pick the potential whose natural variables match the derivative you want: U(S,V), H(S,p), A(T,V) or G(T,p).
Write its exact differential from the definition of the potential.
Read the coefficient of each differential as a partial derivative; this fixes M, N, x and y.
Apply Euler's criterion, keeping every minus sign that sits in front of a coefficient.
Check the subscripts: they must be the two natural variables of that potential.

sections.h3: The four relations and entropy from p-v-T data

blocks.text: H = U + pV, A = U − TS and G = H − TS each give an exact differential (see 4.3). The same steps on each produce the remaining three Maxwell relations.
Two of the four put entropy on the left with T held fixed. Those are the working relations, because the right-hand sides are ordinary p-v-T slopes:

blocks.where: lowercase s and v are per unit mass, in kJ/(kg·K) and m³/kg; the first gives entropy change from a volume change, the second from a pressure change, both at constant temperature.

blocks.text: The second one is the standard route to isothermal entropy change. For an ideal gas v = RT/p, so (∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> = R/p and (∂s/∂p)<sub>T</sub> = −R/p. Integrating from p₁ to p₂ at constant T gives Δs = −R ln(p₂/p₁).
The same substitution gives the enthalpy relation. Start from dh = T ds + v dp and hold T constant:

blocks.where: h is specific enthalpy in kJ/kg and v is specific volume in m³/kg; the term v − T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> is the enthalpy departure from ideal-gas behaviour.

blocks.text: For an ideal gas T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> = v, so the departure vanishes and enthalpy depends on temperature alone. For a real gas it does not, which is why steam tables need pressure as well as temperature.

Push a gas through a throttle — a porous plug or a slightly open valve. It is adiabatic, does no shaft work and its kinetic energy is unchanged, so h₁ = h₂: throttling is a constant-enthalpy process. The Joule-Kelvin coefficient asks whether the temperature falls.

blocks.where: μ<sub>JK</sub> is in K/kPa, c<sub>p</sub> is the specific heat at constant pressure in kJ/(kg·K), and the bracket is the enthalpy departure term above.

blocks.text: Derivation: write dh = c<sub>p</sub> dT + [v − T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>] dp. Set dh = 0 and solve for (∂T/∂p)<sub>h</sub>.

For an ideal gas v = RT/p, so T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> = v and μ<sub>JK</sub> = 0 exactly. Throttling an ideal gas drops its pressure and leaves its temperature alone. A real gas has μ<sub>JK</sub> > 0 below its inversion temperature (it cools, which is what a refrigerator or an air liquefier wants) and μ<sub>JK</sub> < 0 above it (it warms).

Only a few universities teach the van der Waals result. For one mole, μ<sub>JK</sub> ≈ (2a/RT − b)/c<sub>p</sub>, where a is the attraction constant in Pa·m⁶/mol², b is the co-volume in m³/mol and c<sub>p</sub> is in J/(mol·K). Setting μ<sub>JK</sub> = 0 gives the inversion temperature T<sub>i</sub> = 2a/(Rb).

figure.caption: The coefficient of each differential is a partial derivative; equating the two mixed second derivatives of U turns those coefficients into the first Maxwell relation.

spec.title: From an exact differential to a Maxwell relation
spec.aria: Reading the coefficients of dU as derivatives and equating the two mixed second derivatives gives one Maxwell relation; the same steps on H, A and G give the other three.

examples.question: Air is treated as an ideal gas with R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K). It is compressed isothermally at 300 K from 1 bar to 5 bar. Using a Maxwell relation, find the entropy change per kg.
steps: Pick the relation linking s, T and p. From dG = −s dT + v dp, the Maxwell relation is (∂s/∂p)<sub>T</sub> = −(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>.
For an ideal gas v = RT/p, so (∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> = R/p.
Hence (∂s/∂p)<sub>T</sub> = −R/p, and at constant T, ds = −R dp/p.
Integrate from p₁ = 1 bar to p₂ = 5 bar: Δs = −R ln(p₂/p₁) = −0.287 × ln 5 kJ/(kg·K).
Round to −0.462 kJ/(kg·K). The sign is negative because squeezing the gas into a smaller volume at constant temperature lowers its entropy.
examples.answer: Δs = −0.462 kJ/(kg·K); the entropy falls because the gas is compressed into a smaller volume at constant temperature.
examples.check:
import math
R = 0.287
p1 = 1.0
p2 = 5.0
ds = -R * math.log(p2 / p1)
print(round(ds, 3))

examples.question: Find the Joule-Kelvin coefficient of an ideal gas and say what it means for a throttle.
steps: For an ideal gas, v = RT/p.
Differentiate at constant p: (∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> = R/p = v/T.
A gas at the hot end of the bracket gets no temperature change on throttling, though its pressure still drops.
examples.answer: μ_JK = 0 exactly for an ideal gas; throttling changes pressure but not temperature.

traps: Sign slip: (∂s/∂v)<sub>T</sub> = (∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub> and (∂T/∂p)<sub>S</sub> = (∂V/∂S)<sub>p</sub> carry no minus, the other two do. Writing (∂s/∂p)<sub>T</sub> = +(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> is the commonest error; re-derive from the potential instead of memorising signs.

Wrong subscript: the subscript names the variable held constant and must match the potential you started from. (∂s/∂p)<sub>T</sub> comes from G; (∂s/∂p)<sub>h</sub> is a different quantity used in throttling.
Mixing V and v: the relations hold for total volume in m³ or specific volume in m³/kg, never both in one problem — the mismatch costs a factor of mass.
Reading μ<sub>JK</sub> = 0 as 'no throttling': for an ideal gas the pressure falls and enthalpy stays constant; only the temperature is unchanged.

Using the relations outside their assumption: they belong to a simple compressible system with two independent properties, so a system with magnetic, electrical or surface work does not obey them as written.

quiz.q: State Euler's criterion for the exactness of dz = M dx + N dy.
quiz.a: If dz is exact then (∂M/∂y)<sub>x</sub> = (∂N/∂x)<sub>y</sub>, that is, the two mixed second derivatives of z are equal.

quiz.q: Write the Maxwell relation that comes from dA = −S dT − p dV.
Why is a Maxwell relation useful in practice?
quiz.a: It replaces an entropy derivative, which cannot be measured directly, by a p-v-T slope that can be measured or read from an equation of state or a property table.

quiz.q: An ideal gas with R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K) is compressed isothermally at 350 K from 1 bar to 10 bar. Find the entropy change per kg.
Show that (∂h/∂p)<sub>T</sub> = 0 for an ideal gas.
quiz.a: v = RT/p, so (∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> = R/p and T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> = RT/p = v. Then v − T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> = 0, so enthalpy depends on temperature only.

quiz.q: A gas entering a throttle has μ<sub>JK</sub> > 0. What happens to its temperature, and why does that matter in a liquefier?
quiz.a: Pressure falls through the throttle, so a positive μ<sub>JK</sub> means temperature also falls. A liquefier relies on this self-cooling; if μ<sub>JK</sub> were negative the gas would warm and cooling would have to be arranged some other way, which is why the operating point must stay below the inversion temperature.

quiz.q: Why is μ<sub>JK</sub> exactly zero for an ideal gas but not for a van der Waals gas?
quiz.a: For an ideal gas v is exactly proportional to T at fixed p, so T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> cancels v. The van der Waals equation adds attraction (a) and finite molecular size (b), which break that proportionality and leave μ<sub>JK</sub> ≈ (2a/RT − b)/c<sub>p</sub>, zero only at the inversion temperature 2a/(Rb).

beyond: Not for the exam. Steam tables and refrigerant charts are built by fitting one fundamental equation — Helmholtz energy as a function of density and temperature — and then differentiating it; every entry, entropy included, comes out through this same mixed-derivative logic. The IAPWS formulation for water and the reference equations for carbon dioxide work this way. The departure term v − T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> appears in every real-gas enthalpy chart. Search 'fundamental equation of state', 'enthalpy departure function' and 'Joule-Thomson inversion curve'.
